cve_explanation: windows-build-tools is a module for installing C++ Build Tools for Windows using npm. windows-build-tools versions below 1.0.0 download resources over HTTP, which leaves it vulnerable to MITM attacks. It may be possible to cause remote code execution (RCE) by swapping out the requested resources with an attacker controlled copy if the attacker is on the network or positioned in between the user and the remote server.
original_explanations: Download of sensitive file through insecure connection

detected_issues.explanation: Build Tools installer downloaded over plain HTTP and executed as Administrator — src/constants.js hardcodes the Visual Studio C++ Build Tools installer URL as plain HTTP: installerUrl: 'http://download.microsoft.com/download/5/f/7/5f7acaeb-8363-451f-9425-68a90f98b238/visualcppbuildtools_full.exe'. src/download.js fetches this URL with nugget (src/download.js:38) into %USERPROFILE%\.windows-build-tools\BuildTools_Full.exe, and src/install/launch.js then runs ps1/launch-installer.ps1, which executes ./BuildTools_Full.exe (and is required to run from an administrative PowerShell). Because the download is unauthenticated HTTP with no integrity check (no hash/signature verification), an attacker positioned on the network path (MITM, hostile Wi-Fi, DNS/ARP spoofing) can substitute a malicious executable for visualcppbuildtools_full.exe. The package's postinstall runs automatically on `npm install`, so this yields arbitrary code execution with Administrator privileges on the victim's Windows machine.

TLS certificate validation disabled for all installer downloads — src/download.js sets strictSSL: false in the nugget options used for every download (line 34). This disables TLS certificate-chain/hostname validation, so even the HTTPS sources (e.g. the python mirror at https://www.python.org) are fetched without verifying the server's certificate. An attacker able to intercept the connection can present a self-signed/mismatched certificate, serve an arbitrary installer payload, and have it written to disk and subsequently executed by the installer scripts (BuildTools_Full.exe is launched from an administrative PowerShell). The failure to validate certificates removes the last transport-authenticity control for the downloaded executable/installer, enabling man-in-the-middle remote code execution.

cve_explanation: Http-proxy is a proxying library. Because of the way errors are handled in versions before 0.7.0, an attacker that forces an error can crash the server, causing a denial of service.

detected_issues.explanation: Uncaught error in middleware stack crashes the proxy (denial of service) — exports.stack() wraps each middleware layer and gives it a next(err) callback. When a middleware calls next(err) - for example because attacker-controlled request data causes a routing, parsing, or authentication middleware to fail - the handler executes `throw err` synchronously inside the http/https server's 'request' listener. Nothing in the request path catches it, so Node.js raises uncaughtException and terminates the whole proxy process. A remote attacker who can force any middleware to error (malformed request, failing upstream, bad input to a middleware) therefore crashes the server: CWE-730 denial of service via an uncaught exception (CWE-248). The upstream fix for this vulnerability (node-http-proxy 0.7.0) replaces the throw with a proper 500 'Internal Server Error' response.

Affected versions of `randomatic` generate random values using a cryptographically weak psuedo-random number generator. This may result in predictable values instead of random values as intended.




## Recommendation

Update to version 3.0.0 or later.

cve_explanation:
Affected versions of `hostr` are vulnerable to directory traversal which allows attackers to read files outside the current directory by sending `../` in the url path for GET requests.

Fix by resolving the path and verifying it stays within the intended document root (e.g. `path.resolve` plus a prefix check).

cve_explanation:
Affected versions of `pidusage` pass unsanitized input to `child_process.exec()`, resulting in arbitrary code execution in the `ps` method.
 
This package is vulnerable to this PoC on Darwin, SunOS, FreeBSD, and AIX.

Windows and Linux are not vulnerable. 

## Proof of Concept
```
var pid = require('pidusage');
pid.stat('1 && /usr/local/bin/python');
```


## Recommendation

Update to version 1.1.5 or later.
original_explanations: Unsafe shell command constructed from library input

detected_issues.explanation: OS command injection via pid parameter — The ps() function builds a shell command by concatenating the caller-supplied pid directly into a string and passes it to child_process.exec: exec('ps -o pcpu,rss -p ' + pid, ...). This is the command-injection flaw tracked as CVE-2017-16034; the fix is to validate that pid is a number and avoid the shell, e.g. use execFile/spawn with an argument array.

This is the same code path and vulnerability instance described in the CVE.

Fix: avoid the nullable alternation, e.g. trim with two anchored regexes (/^\s+/ and /\s+$/) or a linear trim so no unbounded quantifier backtracks from many positions.

Versions of `mpath` before 0.5.1 are vulnerable to prototype pollution. Provided certain input `mpath` can add or modify properties of the `Object` prototype. These properties will be present on all objects.

No segment is filtered against the dangerous keys `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype`. An attacker who can influence the path (e.g. a MongoDB-style update key or any API that passes user-controlled field names to mpath.set) can therefore traverse into the prototype chain and write to it. For example, `mpath.set('__proto__.polluted', 'yes', {})` and `mpath.set('constructor.prototype.polluted2', 'yes2', {})` both modify Object.prototype, as verified locally: subsequently `({}).polluted === 'yes'` and `({}).polluted2 === 'yes2'`. This is prototype pollution (CWE-1321): it corrupts every object in the process, enabling denial of service and, in applications that later merge or branch on object properties, remote code execution or authentication/authorization bypass. Note that mpath.get/has/unset share the same unfiltered traversal and mpath.get also resolves `__proto__`, but set() is the write sink that makes pollution possible.

cve_explanation: index.js in the ssri module before 5.2.2 for Node.js is prone to a regular expression denial of service vulnerability in strict mode functionality via a long base64 hash string.

cve_explanation: In the npm package semantic-release before version 17.2.3, secrets that would normally be masked by `semantic-release` can be accidentally disclosed if they contain characters that become encoded when included in a URL. In fast-cvs before version 4.3.6 there is a possible ReDoS vulnerability (Regular Expression Denial of Service) when using ignoreEmpty option when parsing. This has been patched in `v4.3.6` You will only be affected by this if you use the `ignoreEmpty` parsing option. With a path such as `__proto__.polluted` (or `constructor.prototype.polluted`), the loop reaches `Object.prototype`/the constructor's prototype: at line 65 `isObj(object['__proto__'])` is true so it is not replaced, then at line 70 `object[p] = value` writes the attacker's value onto `Object.prototype`. Any application that passes an untrusted key/path into set() (e.g. merging user-supplied settings or query parameters) lets the attacker add or overwrite properties inherited by every object in the process, which can lead to denial of service, authentication/authorization bypass, or remote code execution in code that later invokes the polluted property. Verified: dotProp.set({}, '__proto__.polluted', 'yes') makes ({}).polluted === 'yes', and dotProp.set({}, 'constructor.prototype.polluted2', 'yes2') likewise pollutes Object.prototype.

judge_reasoning: The finding describes prototype pollution in dot-prop's set() function, matching the CVE's description of allowing attackers to add arbitrary properties to JavaScript objects via __proto__/constructor paths. It identifies the exact vulnerability instance at index.js around lines 65-70, which matches the recorded weakness location at line 70. The finding describes the same security impact (prototype pollution), same attack pattern (using __proto__ or constructor.prototype paths), and the same code path in the set() function.

cve_explanation: A denial of service vulnerability exists in Fastify v2.14.1 and v3.0.0-rc.4 that allows a malicious user to trigger resource exhaustion (when the allErrors option is used) with specially crafted schemas.

detected_issues.explanation: Ajv compiled with allErrors:true enables denial of service via crafted request data — buildSchemaCompiler creates the private Ajv instance with allErrors: true as a default; fastify's ajv.customOptions defaults to {} (fastify.js:78-81), so this is NOT overridden for a normal server. For every route that declares a body, querystring, params, or headers JSON schema, validate() (lib/validation.js validateParam/validate) runs this Ajv validator on attacker-controlled request data before the handler executes. Because allErrors is enabled, Ajv does not short-circuit on the first validation failure: it evaluates and collects every failing error. A malicious client can send a request crafted against a route's schema (for example a large payload, or input exercising deeply nested/combinatorial oneOf/anyOf branches) so that validation accumulates an unbounded number of error objects, exhausting CPU and memory per request and causing denial of service. The upstream fix for CVE-2020-8192 (fastify 2.15.1, commit setting allErrors:false with the comment 'When set to true, a DoS attack is possible') changes exactly this line.

judge_reasoning: The finding identifies the exact vulnerability: Ajv compiled with allErrors:true in lib/validation.js causing resource exhaustion via specially crafted schemas/requests. It matches the CVE's security impact (denial of service), attack pattern (resource exhaustion when allErrors option is used), and identifies the same code path in the same file (lib/validation.js) where the benchmark records the weakness. The finding even explicitly references CVE-2020-8192 and the fix.

cve_explanation: A buffer over-read vulnerability exists in bl <4.0.3, <3.0.1, <2.2.1, and <1.2.3 which could allow an attacker to supply user input (even typed) that if it ends up in consume() argument and can become negative, the BufferList state can be corrupted, tricking it into exposing uninitialized memory via regular .slice() calls.
original_explanations: Buffer over-read vulnerability resulting in exposure of uninitialized memory

detected_issues.explanation: Uninitialized memory disclosure via negative/NaN consume() argument (CVE-2020-8244) — BufferList.prototype.consume() does not validate its argument. A negative or NaN `bytes` value fails the `bytes >= this._bufs[0].length` test at line 236, so execution falls into the else branch that runs `this._bufs[0] = this._bufs[0].slice(bytes)` and `this.length -= bytes` (lines 241-242). With a negative value this.length is increased beyond the number of bytes actually stored, corrupting the BufferList's internal accounting. Later slice()/copy() calls trust this.length: on the multi-buffer path copy() performs Buffer.concat(this._bufs, this.length) (or Buffer.allocUnsafe(len)), allocating a buffer larger than the real data and returning heap memory that BufferList never wrote, i.e. disclosing uninitialized process memory. Reproduced: create a BufferList from two 8-byte buffers (length 16), call consume(-8) -> this.length becomes 24, then slice(0, 24) returns 24 bytes whose trailing 8 bytes are uninitialized heap contents. Any application that passes an attacker-influenced value (for example a length parsed from network input) to consume() exposes process memory. Fixed upstream by rejecting non-positive values (Math.trunc + <= 0 guard) in bl 2.2.1/3.0.1/4.0.3.

judge_reasoning: The finding describes exactly CVE-2020-8244: a buffer over-read vulnerability in bl.js where consume() doesn't validate its argument, allowing negative values to corrupt BufferList state and expose uninitialized memory via slice() calls. The finding identifies the same code path (consume() function leading to memory disclosure through slice/copy), the same security impact (uninitialized memory exposure), and the same attack pattern (negative consume argument). While the finding points to line 234 instead of the benchmark's line 189, both are part of the same vulnerability instance in the same file.

detected_issues.explanation: DOM-based XSS via unsanitized link URL (javascript: scheme) — The Link decorator reads the link URL straight from the Draft.js entity data (contentState.getEntity(entityKey).getData().url at line 51) and renders it unescaped as the href of an anchor (<a href={url} target={targetOption}>) at line 59. The URL is attacker-controlled: the link target is taken verbatim from the editor's link text field (src/controls/Link/Component/index.js addLink/updateValue) and from the entity data embedded in the editor content state (e.g. pasted or loaded content), and no scheme validation or sanitization exists anywhere in the repository. React does not block javascript: URLs in an href, so an attacker who can supply content containing a LINK entity whose url is 'javascript:...' causes arbitrary JavaScript to execute in the victim's origin when the link is clicked. The same unvalidated value is also passed to window.open(url, 'blank') in openLink (line 35), executing in the opened context. Impact: script execution in the application's origin, enabling session/credential theft and actions as the victim.
